claims.text: The protective coating is a dual-phase FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy in the as-deposited state.
The as-deposited coating may contain nanoscale precipitates or segregated solute clusters.
Fine, coherent precipitates are present within the alloy matrix.
The precipitates form stable interfaces with both the FCC and BCC phases.
Fine, coherent precipitates govern the coating's creep resistance.
The precipitates act as pinning sites that impede dislocation motion during continuous loading.
Reduced dislocation mobility increases the effective threshold for creep.
Precipitate-mediated dislocation pinning delays progressive plastic flow.
A higher precipitate density or an optimal precipitate distribution will produce a lower creep strain rate than a precipitate-lean or homogenized baseline.
A higher precipitate density or an optimal precipitate distribution will delay the onset of tertiary creep relative to the baseline.
The mechanism operates under sustained stress at temperatures that do not cause precipitate coarsening or dissolution.
Precipitate coarsening or dissolution at higher temperatures degrades the precipitate structure and disables the proposed creep-resistance mechanism.
Processing can be adjusted to create precipitate-rich and precipitate-lean coating groups for a controlled comparison.
Rapid quenching or alloying modifications can be used to minimize precipitate formation.

Statistically indistinguishable creep behavior between precipitate-rich and precipitate-lean coatings, or worse behavior in the precipitate-rich coating, would falsify the proposed governing role of fine precipitates.
